blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 13 (Thermal Physics), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question of 5 marks (define, explain, derive) is followed by a numerical of 3 marks on the same topic. Each question has a model answer; the numericals are solved step by step.

blocks.prompt: 1 What is Brownian motion? Explain its cause and the factors on which its speed depends. Also state the basic assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Brownian motion: the random, irregular (zig-zag) motion of small particles suspended in a fluid, caused by collisions with the fluid's molecules. In 1827 the botanist Robert Brown saw pollen particles in a liquid moving randomly under a microscope. Einstein explained it in 1905 and J Perrin verified it experimentally in 1908.

Cause: a molecule changes its path after each collision. Each collision transfers or exchanges momentum and energy, so a particle that keeps on being struck follows a random, zig-zag path (Fig. 13.1). It is a simple model of randomness.

Factors:
(1) Mass/size: the transfer of momentum is inversely proportional to the mass of the particles, so lighter particles obtain greater speeds.
(2) Viscosity: the speed of the particles is inversely proportional to the viscosity (internal friction) of the fluid; low viscosity gives faster Brownian movement.

Assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases:
(1) A gas consists of a very large number of tiny spherical particles far apart compared to their sizes; their own volume is negligible.
(2) The particles are in constant rapid motion in random directions.
(3) Collisions between particles and with the container walls are perfectly elastic.
(4) There are no forces of attraction or repulsion between particles except during collisions.
(5) The average kinetic energy of the particles depends on the temperature of the gas.

book_ref.quote: There are various reasons and causes of this motion which are given as under:

blocks.prompt: 2 A cylinder of volume 0.025 m³ contains an ideal gas at a pressure of 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 350 K. Find (i) the number of gas molecules and (ii) the number of moles. (k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹, N_A = 6.02 × 10²³) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use PV = Nk_BT for the number of molecules, then n = N/N_A.

book_ref.quote: The number of moles in terms of number of particle N is defined as; n = N/N_A, then

blocks.prompt: 3 A single molecule of mass m moves with velocity component vₓ inside a cubical box of side L. Using the kinetic theory, obtain expressions for (i) its change in momentum on striking a wall, (ii) the time between its successive collisions with the same wall, (iii) the average force on the wall and (iv) the pressure it exerts. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Model: one molecule of mass m moves back and forth in a cube of side L (Fig. 13.2), colliding elastically with the walls.

(i) Change in momentum: it strikes a face along the x-axis with momentum mvₓ and rebounds with −mvₓ.
Δp = −mvₓ − (mvₓ) = −2mvₓ

(ii) Time between collisions: it travels a distance 2L between consecutive collisions with the same wall.
Δt = 2L/vₓ ... (13.3)

(iii) Force: by Newton's second law, force = rate of change of momentum. The force of the molecule on the wall is opposite to the force of the wall on the molecule (Newton's third law), so we take the magnitude:
F = |Δp|/Δt = 2mvₓ/(2L/vₓ) = mvₓ²/L ... (13.4)

(iv) Pressure: the area of the wall is L².
P = F/L² = (mvₓ²/L)/L² = mvₓ²/L³
P = mvₓ²/V ... (13.5)
where V = L³ is the volume of the box. This is the pressure exerted on the wall by one molecule.

book_ref.quote: It is assumed that a single molecule is moving in a cube-like box of each side L

blocks.prompt: 4 An oxygen molecule of mass 5.3 × 10⁻²⁶ kg moves with vₓ = 450 m s⁻¹ inside a cubical box of side 0.10 m. Find (i) the magnitude of its change in momentum at one wall, (ii) the time between its collisions with that wall, (iii) the average force and (iv) the pressure it exerts on the wall. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use |Δp| = 2mvₓ, Δt = 2L/vₓ, F = |Δp|/Δt and P = F/L².

book_ref.quote: As pressure is force per unit area, exerted on walls of the container

blocks.prompt: 5 Starting from the pressure of one molecule, P = mvₓ²/V, obtain the kinetic-theory expression PV = ⅓Nm<v²> for N molecules. Explain why the mean square velocity is used, and express the result in terms of the density of the gas. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
All molecules: add the contributions of all molecules striking the wall, each with a different speed:
P = (m/V)(v₁ₓ² + v₂ₓ² + v₃ₓ² + ...) ... (13.6)

Why squares: a molecule strikes with vₓ and leaves with −vₓ, so the simple average velocity is zero. To avoid this zero, the velocities are squared before averaging:
<vₓ²> = (v₁ₓ² + v₂ₓ² + ... + v_Nₓ²)/N
so v₁ₓ² + v₂ₓ² + ... = N<vₓ²>, and P = (Nm/V)<vₓ²>.
The square root of the average square is the rms velocity: (vᵣₘₛ)ₓ = √<vₓ²>.

Three directions: the molecules move randomly with the same average speed in all three directions:
<v²> = <vₓ²> + <v_y²> + <v_z²> = 3<vₓ²> ... (13.10)
<vₓ²> = <v²>/3 ... (13.11)

Result:
P = (N/3V)m<v²> ... (13.12)
PV = ⅓Nm<v²> ... (13.13)

In terms of density: the total mass is M = mN, so ρ = M/V = mN/V. Then
P = ⅓ρ<v²>
The pressure of a gas depends on its density and on the mean square speed of its molecules.

book_ref.quote: The total force, we must add up the contributions of all the molecules that strike the wall

blocks.prompt: 6 An ideal gas has a density of 2.4 kg m⁻³ at a pressure of 1.6 × 10⁵ Pa. Find (i) the mean square speed and (ii) the rms speed of its molecules. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Rearrange P = ⅓ρ<v²> for <v²>, then take the square root.

book_ref.quote: This is the pressure of the gas which depends on the density and root mean square of velocity.

blocks.prompt: 7 Show that the pressure of a gas is two-thirds of the average translational kinetic energy of its molecules per unit volume, i.e. P = ⅔N₀<K.E._T>. What do N₀ and <K.E._T> stand for? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Start from the kinetic-theory result:
PV = ⅓Nm<v²> ... (13.13)
P = (mN/3V)<v²>

Write ⅓m<v²> as ⅔ × ½m<v²>:
P = ⅔(N/V)<½mv²>

Let N₀ = N/V, the number of molecules per unit volume:
P = ⅔N₀<½mv²>

<½mv²> = <K.E._T> is the average translational kinetic energy of one molecule, so
P = ⅔N₀<K.E._T>

Meaning: N₀<K.E._T> is the total translational K.E. per unit volume; the pressure equals two-thirds of it. So the pressure rises if either the number of molecules per unit volume or their average K.E. (the temperature) increases.

book_ref.quote: Rearranging the pressure, Eq. (13.13) for P, and substituting the density

blocks.prompt: 8 A gas contains 3.0 × 10²⁵ molecules per cubic metre, and the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule is 5.0 × 10⁻²¹ J. Find (i) the pressure of the gas and (ii) its temperature. (k_B = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use P = ⅔N₀<K.E._T> for pressure and <K.E._T> = (3/2)k_BT for temperature.

book_ref.quote: This force spreads over whole wall area of the container.

blocks.prompt: 9 By equating the gas law with the kinetic-theory expression for pressure, derive the formula for the rms speed of gas molecules, vᵣₘₛ = √(3RT/mN_A). How does the rms speed depend on temperature and on the mass of one mole? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Two expressions for PV:
Gas law: PV = nRT
Kinetic theory: PV = (N/3)m<v²> = (N/3)mvᵣₘₛ²

Equating:
nRT = (N/3)mvᵣₘₛ² ... (13.15)
mvᵣₘₛ² = 3nRT/N

N/n = N_A is the number of molecules in one mole (Avogadro's number), so n/N = 1/N_A:
mvᵣₘₛ² = 3RT/N_A
or ½mvᵣₘₛ² = 3RT/2N_A
or vᵣₘₛ² = 3RT/(mN_A)
vᵣₘₛ = √(3RT/mN_A) ... (13.16)

Here mN_A is the mass of one mole of the gas.

Dependence:
(1) vᵣₘₛ ∝ √T: raising the absolute temperature raises the rms speed (four times T gives twice the speed).
(2) vᵣₘₛ ∝ 1/√(mN_A): at the same temperature a gas with a heavier mole has slower molecules.
Since k_B = R/N_A, the same result is vᵣₘₛ = √(3k_BT/m).

book_ref.quote: We have calculated the pressure of the gas molecule with n (=N/V) molecules

blocks.prompt: 10 The mass of one mole of oxygen is 0.032 kg. Find (i) the rms speed of oxygen molecules at 350 K and (ii) the temperature at which this rms speed would be doubled. (R = 8.31 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use vᵣₘₛ = √(3RT/mN_A); since vᵣₘₛ ∝ √T, doubling the speed needs four times the absolute temperature.

book_ref.quote: However, M/m is simply Avogadro's number

blocks.prompt: 11 Using the rms-speed relation and k_B = R/N_A, obtain the expression <K.E._T> = (3/2)k_BT for the average translational kinetic energy of a gas molecule. Find the value of k_BT at 300 K in joules and in electron volts, and explain why the electron volt is used. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
From the kinetic theory and the gas law (topic 13.4):
mvᵣₘₛ² = 3RT/N_A
The gas constant is related to the Boltzmann constant by k_B = R/N_A, so
mvᵣₘₛ² = 3k_BT
½m<v²> = (3/2)k_BT ... (13.17)

½mvᵣₘₛ² is the average translational kinetic energy <K.E._T> of a molecule. Equivalently
⅔(½mvᵣₘₛ²) = k_BT ... (13.18)
<K.E._T> = (3/2)k_BT

Meaning: the average translational K.E. of the molecules is a constant times the absolute temperature, so the temperature of a gas is a direct measure of the average translational K.E. of its molecules.

Value at 300 K:
k_BT = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ × 300 K = 4.14 × 10⁻²¹ J
With k_B = 8.62 × 10⁻⁵ eV K⁻¹: k_BT = 8.62 × 10⁻⁵ × 300 = 0.026 eV

Electron volt: such energies are very small in joules, so the electron volt is used. 1 eV is the kinetic energy of an electron accelerated through a voltage difference of one volt; 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.

blocks.prompt: 13 What is statistical physics? Write the Boltzmann distribution law, explain each symbol in it, and state what it tells us about the populations of energy states. Also state the average kinetic energy of a molecule at temperature T. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Statistical physics: for a large number of molecules we use statistical physics, the branch of physics that uses probability theory. Atoms and molecules of a system may exist in different energy states (levels) E₁, E₂, E₃, ... because of their different speeds.

Background: in 1860 James Clerk Maxwell derived an expression for the distribution of molecular speeds at thermal equilibrium, confirmed by experiment about 60 years later. Boltzmann derived the Boltzmann kinetic equation, which describes dynamic processes in gases with a large number of molecules.

Boltzmann distribution law:
N₂/N₁ = e^(−ΔE/k_BT) ... (13.19)
N₁, N₂ = populations of the lower and higher energy states
ΔE = E₂ − E₁ = energy difference between the states
k_B = Boltzmann constant, T = absolute temperature
e^(−ΔE/k_BT) = Boltzmann factor

Meaning: the probability of finding molecules in a particular energy state varies exponentially as the negative of the energy divided by k_BT. Since ΔE > 0, N₂/N₁ < 1: more particles reside in lower energy states than in higher ones. The law is important in the statistical mechanics of a large number of molecules.

Average energy: a molecule undergoes billions of collisions every second, each changing its speed and K.E., but the average kinetic energy at temperature T is
E_av = (3/2)k_BT ... (13.20)
where k_B is effectively the gas constant per molecule.

book_ref.quote: So far we know that kinetic theory of gases is used to determine the pressure of the ideal gas

blocks.prompt: 14 Two energy levels of the molecules of a gas are separated by 0.052 eV. The gas is at 300 K and the lower level holds 1.0 × 10²⁰ molecules. Find (i) k_BT in eV, (ii) the Boltzmann factor and (iii) the number of molecules in the higher level. (k_B = 8.62 × 10⁻⁵ eV K⁻¹) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find k_BT, then the Boltzmann factor e^(−ΔE/k_BT) = N₂/N₁, and multiply by N₁.

book_ref.quote: is important in describing the statistical mechanics of a large number of molecules

blocks.final_answer: k_BT = 0.0259 eV; Boltzmann factor ≈ 0.134; N₂ ≈ 1.3 × 10¹⁹ molecules

blocks.prompt: 15 What are neutron stars? Describe their main features, explain what pulsars are and how their radiation is produced, and explain why the magnetic field becomes very strong when a star collapses into a neutron star. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Neutron stars: dense remnants formed when the iron core of a star roughly ten times the Sun's mass collapses under gravity in a supernova explosion. They are among the densest known objects in the universe, second only to black holes.

Features:
(1) Because of the extremely high density, matter inside them behaves like a degenerate gas.
(2) Their strong gravitational fields make them challenging to model, and the nearest are many parsecs away, so direct study is difficult.
(3) NASA estimates there may be up to a billion neutron stars in the Milky Way.
(4) One teaspoon of neutron-star material would have a mass over 5.5 × 10¹² kg; the whole Earth at this density would fit in a sphere 305 m in diameter.

Pulsars: many observed neutron stars are relatively young, rotate rapidly and emit beams of radiation; these are pulsars. Pulsar radiation is believed to be produced when strong magnetic fields channel matter toward the magnetic poles of the neutron star.

Strong magnetic field: when a star collapses to form a neutron star, not only its mass but also its magnetic field is compressed. The field lines are squeezed closer together during the collapse of the stellar core, and closer field lines mean a stronger field, so the field is greatly intensified.

book_ref.quote: Due to their extremely high density, matter inside neutron stars behaves like a degenerate gas

blocks.prompt: 16 A massive star has mass 3 × 10³⁰ kg, radius 6 × 10⁸ m and internal pressure 1.0 × 10¹⁵ Pa. Using P_g ≈ GM²/R⁴, find its gravitational pressure and decide whether the star is stable. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Compute P_g ≈ GM²/R⁴ and compare it with the internal pressure; the larger one decides contraction or expansion.

book_ref.quote: Calculate gravitational pressure and compare it with internal pressure

steps: P_g/P_internal = 4.6 × 10¹⁵/1.0 × 10¹⁵ ≈ 4.6, so gravity is stronger: the star is not stable and contracts (it may collapse into a neutron star or black hole)
blocks.final_answer: P_g ≈ 4.6 × 10¹⁵ Pa > 1.0 × 10¹⁵ Pa: the star contracts (not stable)

blocks.prompt: 17 Describe the formation of the Sun and the stages of its life cycle. In which stage is it now, and why is the Sun important in thermal physics? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The Sun is the nearest star to Earth and the main source of heat and light for our planet.

Formation: about 4.6 billion years ago the Sun formed from a huge cloud of gas and dust called a solar nebula. Gravitational contraction raised the temperature at the centre and a protostar was formed. When the core became extremely hot, nuclear fusion started, changing hydrogen into helium and releasing a large amount of energy.

Life stages (Fig. 13.5):
nebula → protostar → main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf

Present stage: the Sun is in the main sequence stage, producing heat and light by converting hydrogen into helium.

Stability: a star stays in equilibrium while the inward gravitational pressure (P_g ≈ GM²/R⁴) is balanced by its internal pressure. If gravity is stronger the star contracts; if the internal pressure dominates it expands and may evolve into a red giant.

Importance in thermal physics: the Sun is a natural source of enormous heat energy and transfers this energy mainly by radiation.

book_ref.quote: When the core became extremely hot, nuclear fusion started

blocks.prompt: 18 A star has mass 2 × 10³⁰ kg, radius 1 × 10⁹ m and internal pressure 5 × 10¹⁴ Pa. Using P_g ≈ GM²/R⁴, find its gravitational pressure and state what will happen to the star. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Compute P_g and compare with the internal pressure.

book_ref.quote: A star has mass 1 × 10³⁰ kg, radius 1 × 10⁹ m and internal pressure 5 × 10¹⁴ Pa.

steps: P_internal/P_g = 5 × 10¹⁴/2.7 × 10¹⁴ ≈ 1.9, so the internal pressure dominates: the star expands and may evolve into a red giant
blocks.final_answer: P_g ≈ 2.7 × 10¹⁴ Pa < 5 × 10¹⁴ Pa: the star expands (may become a red giant)

blocks.prompt: 19 How does a star form from a nebula and reach equilibrium? Write the hydrostatic equation of a star, explain every symbol in it, and explain the role of nuclear fusion in keeping the star in equilibrium. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Formation: all stars form from clouds of gas and dust called nebulae or molecular clouds. As a cloud contracts its density and temperature increase because the K.E. of the particles rises (K.E. ∝ T); this is a protostar. After millions of years it becomes a star on reaching equilibrium. Fig. 13.4 shows the competition between gravity and pressure.

Equilibrium: as the temperature rises the internal pressure also rises. A stable star forms when the inward gravitational force is exactly balanced by the outward pressure. This is described by the hydrostatic equation:
ΔP/Δr = −GMᵣρᵣ/r²

Symbols:
P = pressure inside the star (force per unit area)
ΔP/Δr = rate of change of pressure with radius (from the centre outward)
r = distance from the centre of the star
G = gravitational constant (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)
Mᵣ = mass enclosed within radius r
ρᵣ = density at radius r
Negative sign: pressure decreases outward while gravity pulls inward.
The equation ensures the star neither collapses under gravity nor expands indefinitely. If gravity > internal pressure the star contracts; if gravity < internal pressure it expands.

Role of fusion: as the core temperature rises, nuclear fusion begins: hydrogen nuclei combine to form helium, releasing an immense amount of energy. This sustains and powers the star for most of its life, maintains equilibrium against gravitational collapse, and gradually raises the internal temperature, so the star begins to expand.

book_ref.quote: As the temperature increases, the internal pressure also rises.

blocks.prompt: 20 At a distance r = 5 × 10⁸ m from the centre of a star, the mass enclosed is 1.0 × 10³⁰ kg and the density is 1.4 × 10³ kg m⁻³. Using the hydrostatic equation, find (i) the rate of change of pressure with radius at this point and (ii) the approximate drop in pressure over the next 1000 m outward. (G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Substitute into ΔP/Δr = −GMᵣρᵣ/r², then multiply by Δr = 1000 m.

book_ref.quote: ΔP/Δr is the rate of change of pressure with radius

blocks.final_answer: ΔP/Δr ≈ −3.7 × 10⁵ Pa m⁻¹; pressure drops by about 3.7 × 10⁸ Pa over 1000 m

blocks.prompt: 21 Describe the later stages in the life of stars: the red giant stage, fusion of heavier elements, and the different ends of low or intermediate mass stars, very massive stars and red dwarfs. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Red giant: with further increase in temperature and changes in core composition, the star may expand significantly to become a red giant. Stars with at least about half the Sun's mass can then start helium fusion in their cores, producing heavier elements such as carbon and oxygen. In more massive stars fusion continues in successive stages, forming increasingly complex nuclei up to iron.

Final fate depends mainly on mass. Once a star exhausts its nuclear fuel it can no longer support itself against gravitational collapse.

(1) Low and intermediate mass stars: the core contracts into a dense white dwarf, while the outer layers are expelled into space as a planetary nebula.
(2) Stars about ten times the Sun's mass: after the red supergiant stage they undergo a dramatic supernova explosion; the inert iron core collapses under gravity, forming a neutron star or a black hole.
(3) Red dwarfs: because of their low mass and highly efficient fuel use they evolve very slowly; the universe is not yet old enough for any red dwarf to have completed its life. Models show they will become hotter and more luminous, then exhaust their hydrogen and become low mass white dwarfs.

Lifetimes range from a few million years to trillions of years: the least massive stars (red dwarfs) live longest, while the most massive stars live only a few million years.

book_ref.quote: With further increases in temperature and changes in core composition

blocks.prompt: 22 A supernova remnant is observed at a distance of 2.5 parsec. Express this distance (i) in light years and (ii) in kilometres. (1 parsec ≈ 3.26 light years ≈ 31 trillion km) (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Multiply the distance in parsec by each conversion factor.

book_ref.quote: one parsec is approximately 3.26 light years

steps: Distance in light years = 2.5 × 3.26 = 8.15 light years
